I think of the total war games on the tactical level as being about area denial- you need to have enough siege units to make it impossible for the enemy to stay at long range, enough ranged units to make it impossible for them to stay at medium range, and enough melee to make it impossible for them to attack in melee (once they get there after being shot by all the above). You also need shock cavalry to hit their infantry from behind once they're engaged, hit their isolated siege units if possible to make sure you maintain long range supremacy, and most importantly, to massacre all their routing troops so you don't have to fight the same army again next turn. In practice this usually works out in a full stack of 20 as about 4 siege units, 4-6 shock cavalry, maybe a couple spearmen to catch cavalry charges on if you can't break them with your archers in time, and the rest somewhere around a 60-40 mix of the heaviest infantry available and archers. I accordingly have no use for light infantry, skirmish cavalry (although those can be very annoying to fight against), or melee cavalry with a low charge bonus.

My favorite of the series is Shogun 2, which is under $10 during the summer sale. Empire/Napoleon made it so anything besides line infantry and mortars was a mistake, leading to fairly boring army makeup; and I didn't like the horde mechanics in Attila- playing as a horde wasn't fun for me, and playing against a horde can be annoyingly whack-a-mole. Warhammer puts such a huge importance on race selection and heroes that it's hard to compare to the rest. Shogun 2 had the unique bonuses in provinces that made taking territory affect your optimal army makeup in an interesting way, the unit variety was still good, and the shogun/christianity+muskets mechanics were kind of fun. I did like Rome 1+2 too, though.
